"Yearly check," Naveen said, phone on speaker, papers spread over the bed. "You told me to do it, Harish, so I'm doing it."
"Good. What's changed since last year?" Harish asked.
"New job, so a different office cover. And I got married."
"Then the nominee?"
"Still Papa's name. It should be Meera now, and maybe Papa second." Naveen frowned at the page. "The amount also looks like it was set when I earned half of this."
"Call the helpline tomorrow morning and ask what changes and what it costs. Don't guess."
"I'll take today's date and note what they say."
Next morning Naveen wrote the new nominee and amount in the notebook. It felt finished.

qa.q: What has changed in Naveen's life since last year?
qa.a: Naveen has a new job and got married.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when noticing the amount was set when he earned half as much?
qa.a: Naveen felt a little uneasy and startled, shown by the frown, at how out of date the amount looked.

qa.q: What could Naveen do next year so the review stays useful?
qa.a: Naveen could set a fixed date each year and list any life changes before phoning the helpline.

qa.q: How might Harish have seen Naveen's phone call?
qa.a: Harish probably felt glad and a little proud that Naveen followed the yearly habit, and stayed practical by telling Naveen to ask the helpline.

grounding: The dialogue shows a person, after a job change and a marriage, checking policy amounts and nominees and updating them so cover fits new responsibilities.

passage:
My name's Gargi, and for three years I didn't look at my insurance once. I bought it at twenty-two, in my first job, when the only person relying on me was me. The nominee was my mother. The cover was whatever the office agent suggested.
Then, within eight months, I switched to a new company and got married. It was my sister Seema who asked, at the wedding lunch, 'Who's your nominee now?' I laughed. Then I didn't.
That Sunday I took out every paper. The old employer's group health plan had ended with the job. The term cover was sized for a single fresher with no loan. Now there was Dev, and a flat loan in both our names.
I updated the nominee, joined the new company's health plan with Dev, and booked time with an adviser to recheck the term cover. 'Insurance check' sits in my calendar every January now.

qa.q: What did Seema ask at the wedding lunch?
What did Gargi feel when the laugh stopped?
qa.a: Gargi felt a jolt of worry and some embarrassment, realising the cover and the nominee were still frozen from the first job.

qa.q: Which extra step could Gargi add to the January check, and why?
qa.a: Gargi could keep a one-page list of policies, nominees and renewal dates to go through with Dev, so both know what exists if something happens.

qa.q: How might Dev be affected by the updated cover?
qa.a: Dev is now on the health plan and shares the flat loan, so the review protects Dev too, not only Gargi's mother.

grounding: It shows someone checking nominees and cover after a job change and a marriage, and updating them instead of leaving the first purchase unchanged.

passage:
Benefits desk note, 14 July.
Shankar from the new analytics team came to the desk today holding a folder of old policies. He joined us in May and mentioned he got married in February. He said he had not changed anything since he bought his first term plan and a personal health policy at twenty-two. Together we read each paper. His nominee was still his father. The health policy covered him alone; his wife, Latha, was on no plan at all. He was quiet for a moment, then said, 'So everything is still set for the boy I was then.'
He added Latha to our group health plan on the spot and filled in the nominee change form. For the term cover amount, I suggested he speak to an independent adviser, since the desk does not advise on that. Follow-up booked for August.
Sachin, HR

qa.q: Who was still the nominee on Shankar's policy?
qa.a: His father was still the nominee.

qa.q: What does Shankar's quiet moment suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uneasy and a little embarrassed to see his cover still set for his single, younger self.

qa.q: What could Shankar do so the next review doesn't depend on a visit to the desk?
qa.a: He could set a yearly reminder, perhaps near the wedding anniversary, to check nominees and cover with Latha whenever life changes.

qa.q: What would change for Latha if Shankar had not come to the desk?
qa.a: Latha would have stayed off any health plan and would not be the nominee, leaving her unprotected despite the marriage.

grounding: It shows a benefits desk note about an employee who, after a job change and a marriage, checks nominees and cover and updates them.
